In the strict leakage-reduced sensitivity analysis, AUROC decreased to 0.713 (95% CI 0.682–0.745) and decreased further to 0.625 (95% CI 0.589–0.658) after removal of rs429358 and APOE proxy information. The five-SNP model had modest discrimination (AUROC 0.637; 95% CI 0.605–0.670), whereas the Non-APOE SNP-only model was weak (AUROC 0.533; 95% CI 0.497–0.568). In fold-wise validation permutation analysis of the strict model, Test_Age ranked first overall and rs429358 was the highest-ranking genetic feature; the Non-APOE candidates had small or near-zero mean AUROC decreases after permutation. Conclusions This study presents a Korean WES–WGS exploratory clinical–genomic candidate-evaluation framework. The findings indicate that high multimodal discrimination in clinically enriched AD datasets can reflect diagnostic-proximal clinical separability, while Non-APOE candidate variants should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating model features rather than confirmed susceptibility loci, independent predictors, or causal variants. A second independent Korean cohort with harmonized candidate genotypes and comparable clinical and neuropsychological variables was not available within the present study, precluding direct external replication, and the WES and WGS stages used different clinical endpoints.

title: Post-hoc analyses of amyloid reduction after one year of treatment with donanemab using clinical trial data: prediction of amyloid clearance and association with downstream measurements
abstract: Abstract Background Donanemab is an antibody designed to specifically target modified amyloid that is present only in plaques. An objective of this post hoc study was to identify baseline characteristics associated with 52-week amyloid clearance (AC) with donanemab treatment and to assess the association of AC with downstream biomarkers and clinical efficacy. Methods Data was utilized from TRAILBLAZER-ALZ 2 (placebo: N = 876; donanemab: N = 860), a Phase 3, double-blind, placebo-controlled study, and open-label addendum ( N = 1053) in participants with early symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease (AD). Donanemab-treated participants were split into two subgroups based on their 52-week amyloid level: AC W52 [< 24.1 Centiloids (CL)] and NAC W52 (≥ 24.1 CL). Machine learning and multiple linear regression analyses were utilized to assess baseline characteristics differentiating these subgroups. Placebo-treated participants were matched to AC W52 and NAC W52 participants by propensity score and compared using analysis of covariance or mixed models for repeated measures. Results On average, substantial 52-week amyloid reduction was observed in donanemab-treated participants in both the AC W52 ( N = 443) and NAC W52 ( N = 227) subgroups. Baseline amyloid [mean (SD): 95.8 (32.4) and 120.2 (34.0), respectively], was significantly correlated with 52-week amyloid levels [mean (SD): 4.8 CL (12.5) and 48.2 (22.5) CL, respectively ( p < 0.001)] and was inversely associated with probability of reaching 52-week AC ( p < 0.001). Of the baseline characteristics assessed, lower amyloid was the most important parameter differentiating AC W52 and NAC W52 subgroups, followed by older age, fewer APOE ε4 alleles, and lower body weight. These findings were replicated using open-label addendum data. The AC W52 subgroup, but not the NAC W52 subgroup, had significantly less 76-week tau accumulation than matched placebo (mPBO) ( p < 0.01). Although both subgroups showed significant plasma P-tau217 differences from the corresponding mPBO, the change from baseline was greater in the AC W52 subgroup. At 76 weeks, slowing of clinical progression for the AC W52 and NAC W52 subgroups versus mPBO, as measured by Clinical Dementia Rating Scale–Sum of Boxes, was 29.6% and 28.8%, respectively, and slowing by the integrated AD Rating Scale was 25.9% and 18.8%, respectively. Conclusions Donanemab-mediated 52-week amyloid clearance was associated with slower tau progression. Slowing of clinical progression was observed in both AC W52 and NAC W52 subgroups. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov Identifier: NCT04437511, June 2020.

title: Resting-state beta-band oscillatory dysfunction bridges Alzheimer’s pathology and memory impairment
abstract: Abstract Background Resting-state electroencephalography (rs-EEG) is a promising non-invasive biomarker of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet its role in linking molecular pathology to cognitive impairment remains unclear. We investigated whether rs-EEG spectral activity is associated with amyloid-β and tau pathology and how these measures relate to cognition. Methods Thirty-six biomarker-confirmed participants with amyloid-positive Alzheimer’s disease-related mild cognitive impairment (AD-MCI) and 38 cognitively normal older adults underwent rs-EEG assessment. Patients with AD-MCI additionally received amyloid-β and tau positron emission tomography (PET). Power spectral density across frequency bands was compared between groups. Partial correlation analyses examined associations among PET biomarkers, rs-EEG activity, and cognitive performance measured by the Cognitive Abilities Screening Instrument (CASI). Regression-based mediation analyses were performed with adjustment for age, sex, education, and APOE ε4 status. Results Compared with controls, patients with AD-MCI showed increased delta/theta power and reduced beta power. Greater amyloid burden was associated with lower beta-band activity across multiple regions, whereas higher tau burden was associated with reduced beta activity and regionally increased delta and theta activity. Poorer memory performance was associated with reduced beta activity and increased theta activity. Amyloid burden showed no robust direct association with memory performance; however, it was indirectly associated with memory through beta-band activity. In contrast, tau burden was directly associated with poorer memory, and no significant mediation effects through beta activity were observed. Conclusions Beta-band activity may represent a systems-level correlate linking AD pathology and cognition, with amyloid-β showing indirect associations via network dynamics and tau demonstrating more direct relationships with memory impairment.

title: Causal analysis of Alzheimer’s disease molecular data
abstract: Abstract Background Genome-wide studies have revealed many molecular associations with Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but association alone does not identify cause, mechanism, or treatable target. This review surveys methods used to infer causal relationships from AD molecular data and assesses their core findings. Main body We reviewed causal-inference work applied to AD genetics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, proteomics, and metabolomics, covering Mendelian randomization, probabilistic graphical and Bayesian network models, causal reasoning over knowledge graphs, time-resolved methods including Granger causality, and mediation analysis. Genetic-instrument and network methods have identified candidate causal molecules, mapped pathways, and supported some drug targets. However, several associations reported in observational studies have not been supported by genetic analyses, and apparent disagreements between studies often reflect differences in the estimand, the tissue from which genetic instruments are derived, or assumptions of the methods used. Conclusion Brain-relevant genetic instruments, longitudinal multi-omics, single-cell resolution, and triangulation across methods are needed to separate cause from consequence and to prioritize intervention targets for experimental validation.

title: Triple network effective connectivity imbalance across the Alzheimer’s disease spectrum and its modulation by intermittent theta burst stimulation
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive decline, yet the directed network mechanisms underlying this process and their responsiveness to neuromodulation remain incompletely understood. Guided by the triple network model, we investigated effective connectivity (EC) among the default mode network (DMN), central executive network (CEN), and salience network (SN) across the AD spectrum and examined its modulation by intermittent theta burst stimulation (iTBS). Resting-state functional magnetic resonance imaging data were analyzed from two cohorts: a cross-sectional Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative discovery cohort including 280 participants, and an independent pilot longitudinal interventional cohort including 37 mild cognitive impairment patients randomized to active or sham iTBS. Group independent component analysis (ICA) and spectral dynamic causal modeling were used to estimate EC within the triple network, followed by exploratory imaging-transcriptomic of ICA-derived network maps analysis using the Allen Human Brain Atlas. Across the AD spectrum, seven connections showed significant group differences, indicating DMN-centered network dysregulation, with posterior DMN (pDMN) dysfunction emerging as a central feature. Subsequently, pre- to post-intervention changes in the seven altered connections were compared in the longitudinal cohort, and iTBS was associated with greater decreases in ‘SN-to-aDMN’ and ‘pDMN self-inhibition’, with these changes associated with cognitive improvement. Exploratory imaging-transcriptomic analysis further showed that pDMN spatial topography was associated with cortical gene expression profiles enriched for postsynaptic organization and synaptic regulatory processes. These findings suggest DMN-centered EC alterations across the AD spectrum and provide preliminary support for further evaluation of iTBS as a potential therapeutic strategy.

title: Safety, short-term clinical outcomes, and associated factors of lecanemab: a multicenter real-world study from the Korean Joint Registry for Alzheimer’s Treatment and Diagnostics (JOY-ALZ)
abstract: Identifying patient characteristics and treatment strategies associated with better outcomes of lecanemab is important in clinical practice. We evaluated the real-world safety and short-term outcomes of lecanemab and factors associated with these outcomes using the Korean Joint Registry for Alzheimer’s Treatment and Diagnostics (JOY-ALZ). We analyzed data from 663 participants with Alzheimer’s disease (AD) who received at least one lecanemab infusion at 32 hospitals nationwide. Amyloid-related imaging abnormality (ARIA) analyses included 657 patients who underwent at least one monitoring MRI. Dose titration was used at the clinician’s discretion in 74.7% of APOE ε4 homozygotes, 50.5% of heterozygotes, and 32.7% of noncarriers. ARIA occurred in 106 patients (16.1%): ARIA with edema/effusion (ARIA-E) with or without ARIA with hemorrhage/hemosiderin deposition (ARIA-H) in 27 (4.1%) and isolated ARIA-H in 79 (12.0%). Symptomatic ARIA occurred in four patients (0.6%) with ARIA-E. APOE ε4 homozygosity (hazard ratio [HR] 2.81; 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.06–7.46), higher Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes score (HR 1.18; 95% CI 1.04–1.35), greater number of baseline microhemorrhages (HR 1.69; 95% CI 1.32–2.16), and baseline superficial siderosis (HR 7.45; 95% CI 1.50–37.12) were independently associated with ARIA-E. The incidences of ARIA-E and ARIA-H did not differ between standard-dose and titration-dose groups within each APOE ε4 genotype group. Infusion-related reactions occurred in 26.7% and were less frequent with dose titration. Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) scores declined over time (β = −0.15 points/month, 95% CI − 0.21 to − 0.08; P < 0.001), with less decline in patients with mild cognitive impairment and late-onset AD. Higher baseline plasma p-tau217 levels were associated with greater worsening in functional activities. Amyloid PET negativity was achieved in 23.4% (15/64) at 3–9 months and 27.6% (8/29) at 10–12 months and was independently associated with lower baseline Centiloid values (OR 0.92; 95% CI 0.88–0.96) and higher baseline MMSE scores (OR 1.23; 95% CI 1.04–1.45). Lecanemab showed favorable real-world safety and short-term clinical outcomes. These findings may inform patient selection, ARIA risk stratification, treatment optimization, and biomarker-informed treatment strategies in clinical practice.

title: A phase 2b randomized clinical trial of the oral p38α inhibitor neflamapimod in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB)
abstract: Abstract Background: There is high unmet need in dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB). Neflamapimod, showed clinical activity against cognitive and motor endpoints at a dose of 40mg three-times-daily (TID) in a prior phase 2a study in DLB, most prominently in those without Alzheimer disease (AD) co-pathology, assessed by plasma ptau181. Methods: 16-week randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial, with a 32-week open label extension, conducted at 43 centers in the US, UK and Netherlands. 159 participants with probable DLB by consensus criteria, screened to enrich for patients without AD co-pathology (plasma ptau181≥27.2 pg/mL excluded), randomized between August 2023 and June 2024 to neflamapimod 40mg (80 participants) or matching placebo (79 participants) capsules, TID. Mean age 71.4 (6.1), 85.6% male. Primary outcome measure: change in Clinical Dementia Rating Sum-of-Boxes (CDR-SB). Secondary outcome measures: Timed up and Go test, ADCS Clinical Global Impression of Change, and a study-specific cognitive test battery. Biomarker measures: plasma levels of glial fibrillary acidic protein and neurofilament light chain, and basal forebrain atrophy by structural MRI (sub-study in 18 participants). Results: There was no significant difference between neflamapimod and placebo on the primary outcome measure, change in CDR-SB. There were also no differences seen on secondary clinical outcome measures and the two plasma biomarkers, though in the sub-study, improvement relative to placebo was seen with neflamapimod on change in right basal forebrain volume from baseline to week 16. In exploratory analyses, the treatment group difference in change in CDR-SB favored neflamapimod compared to placebo among participants with low (<21 pg/mL) screening plasma p-tau181. Pharmacokinetic data showed that mean trough neflamapimod plasma drug-concentrations (C trough ) were lower than expected, and treatment effect favoring neflamapimod was seen in participants with C trough above the study median. Discontinuation due to adverse events was 2.5% (2 of 79) with neflamapimod and 1.3% (1 of 80) with placebo Discussion: The phase 2a clinical study findings were not replicated, potentially due to the inclusion of a higher proportion of patients with AD co-pathology than targeted and the use of neflamapimod drug product that did not achieve expected plasma drug concentrations. Registered at clinicaltrials.gov on 17 May 2023 (NCT0586966)

title: Neuronal SORT1 coordinates endosomal homeostasis and neuroinflammation crosstalk to protect against Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: In Alzheimer’s disease (AD), early endosomal dysfunction and chronic neuroinflammation critically shape disease progression, yet the neuronal mechanisms underlying the coordinating intracellular trafficking and microglial immune responses remain poorly defined. Sortilin-1 (SORT1), a neuronal VPS10P-domain receptor implicated in endosomal trafficking, proteostasis, and AD genetic risk, acts as a potential integrator of neuronal homeostasis and neuroimmune signaling. Here, we investigated the role of neuronal SORT1 in regulating endosomal integrity and neuron-microglia communication in AD models. Using a co-culture system of human iPSC-derived neurons and microglia-like cells, we found that neuronal SORT1 deficiency disrupted endosomal trafficking and proteostatic balance, leading to the accumulation of β-C-terminal fragments (β-CTFs) of amyloid precursor protein (APP) and pathological tau species. These neuronal defects were accompanied by heightened microglial pro-inflammatory activation and increased neuronal vulnerability. Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) analyses revealed that SORT1 was dynamically expressed in inflammatory microglial populations, supporting early adaptive activation but declining in late-stage AD, which coincided with chronic neuroinflammation. In contrast, preservation of neuronal SORT1 stabilized endosomal organization, attenuated maladaptive microglial responses, and promoted neuronal survival. Moreover, in the 5xFAD mouse model of AD, AAV-mediated neuronal SORT1 expression reduced DNA damage, decreased microglia-associated neuroinflammation, reduced Aβ plaque burden and improved cognitive performance. Together, these findings establish neuronal SORT1 as a critical regulator that preserves endosomal homeostasis, coordinates neuron-microglia crosstalk, and mitigates neurodegeneration and cognitive decline in AD models, highlighting its potential as a target for early therapeutic intervention. Neuronal SORT1 preserves endosomal homeostasis and restrains neuroinflammation in Alzheimer’s disease

title: In vitro comparison of Aβ-targeting SNIPR, synNotch, and TRUCK for programmable transgene expression
abstract: Abstract Background Chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) are being used to direct cytokine secretion and phagocytosis by immune and glial cells toward amyloid β (Aβ) pathology, effectively adapting oncology-derived cell therapies to Alzheimer’s disease (AD). New synthetic receptor systems can take this approach a step further by enabling cells to deliver genetically encoded therapeutics. Among these systems, T cells Redirected for Universal Cytokine Killing (TRUCKs), synthetic Notch (synNotch), and Synthetic Intramembrane Proteolysis Receptors (SNIPRs) have shown promise in oncology and, as CARs, could potentially be adapted to AD. Methods Here, we compared these receptor systems in vitro using Jurkat cells and human regulatory T cells (Tregs). All receptors shared an Aβ-targeting binding domain derived from Aducanumab (Aduhelm) and were coupled to inducible expression cassettes driving identical transgenes: secreted Metridia luciferase (MetLuc) and a Lecanemab (Leqembi)-based chimeric human–mouse antibody (chLecanemab). To model AD pathology in vitro, cell clones were exposed to oligomer-enriched Aβ (AβO) preparations. In Jurkat cells, TRUCK, synNotch, and SNIPR systems were assessed for basal transcriptional leakage, ligand-independent activation, and ligand-dependent activation using flow cytometry and MetLuc reporter assays. Aβ-dependent production of chLecanemab by synNotch and SNIPR systems was further evaluated in Jurkat cells and human Tregs by immunofluorescence (IF). Results We found that the inducible expression cassettes of all receptor systems exhibited transcriptional leakage. Despite confirmed CAR function and transcriptional competence of 6xNFAT response elements paired with different minimal promoters, none of the TRUCK variants produced AβO-induced output significantly above basal leakage. In contrast, synNotch and SNIPR expressed in Jurkat cells and human Tregs responded robustly to AβO. Conclusions We demonstrate that Aβ-targeting SNIPR and synNotch systems can support Aβ-dependent inducible transgene expression in vitro. Their modular architectures enable straightforward substitution of chLecanemab with alternative therapeutic payloads while preserving Aβ-dependent delivery. Because these receptors are orthogonal, the same sequences we provide can be used across different model species and cell types in further studies without requiring receptor redesign.

title: Neuropsychiatric symptom networks in early- and late-onset Alzheimer's disease
abstract: While early- and late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (AD) are defined by the same pathology, presentation of neuropsychiatric symptoms can differ between groups. In this study, we investigate differences in neuropsychiatric symptom co-occurrence between early-onset (EOAD) and late-onset AD (LOAD) using a network-based approach. This cross-sectional study included 655 EOAD (< 65 years, mean age 58.4 ± 4.5 years; 53% female) and 705 LOAD (≥ 65 years, mean age 70.8 ± 4.0 years; 52% female) participants from the Amsterdam Dementia Cohort ( N = 1360). A symptom network for each group was estimated based on the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (NPI-Q) using Ising models for binary data, with dichotomized NPI items as nodes (present or absent) and edge weights (ω) reflecting the strength of the conditional association between two nodes. Networks were compared between EOAD and LOAD by visual inspection, edge strength, node strength centrality (sum of edges), and by comparing the global network strength between both networks (Network Comparison Test). Apathy and depression were most prevalent in both groups (EOAD: 58%,48%; LOAD: 55%,43%). Although global network strength did not differ significantly between groups ( p > .05), subtle differences in symptom connectivity were observed: in EOAD, aggression-disinhibition (ω = 1.22) and aggression-irritability were the strongest edges (ω = 1.22), with aggression and anxiety showing highest node strength within the EOAD network (3.61 and 3.60, respectively), whereas in LOAD, depression-anxiety was the strongest edge (ω = 1.49), with aggression and disinhibition showing highest node strength within the LOAD network (strength = 3.83 and 3.54, respectively). EOAD and LOAD show largely overlapping neuropsychiatric symptom networks, with subtle differences in how symptoms manifest between groups.

title: Plasma exchange reduces amyloid deposition, modulates neuroinflammation, and microglial response in an advanced stage of pathology in the APP/PS1 mouse model
abstract: Current treatments for Alzheimer’s disease (AD) offer limited benefits, and many amyloid-targeting therapies have failed. This has led to exploring alternative approaches, including plasma exchange (PE) with albumin replacement. While this treatment shows promise as a potential therapy, its effect on Aβ pathology, neuroinflammation, and cognitive function is not yet fully understood. APP/PS1 mice received a monthly PE treatment starting at 11 months of age, when the animals had reached an advanced stage of amyloid pathology in this model. Brain and plasma biomarkers were quantified, and immunofluorescence staining of plaques and microglia was performed. Aged APP/PS1 mice subjected to PE showed significantly reduced insoluble Aβ42 and Aβ40 levels, plaque burden, and overall microglia burden while increasing microglia engagement per plaque. These changes were accompanied by higher plasma Aβ levels. PE altered levels of cytokines linked to AD pathology; however, the neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory markers NSE and GFAP were elevated in both transgenic groups relative to WT controls, but did not differ significantly between PE-treated and sham-treated mice. These findings demonstrate that PE with albumin replacement engages amyloid pathology and the neuroinflammatory milieu in the brain, even at advanced stages of the disease. Whether these changes improved the neurodegenerative state remains unknown. These results, along with our previous report, support the need for further studies on PE treatment for AD, including combination therapies and longitudinal studies at preclinical and clinical stages of the disease.

title: A prospective observational study measuring the stability of plasma pTau181 using the Elecsys Phospho-Tau (181P) plasma immunoassay for early detection of Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Background Plasma tau phosphorylated at threonine 181 (pTau181) is a key blood-based biomarker that correlates with the burden of amyloid-beta (Aβ) pathology in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). The Elecsys ® Phospho-Tau (181P) Plasma (pT181p) immunoassay (Roche Diagnostics International Ltd, Rotkreuz, Switzerland) is intended for use as an aid in the early detection of Aβ pathology in adults ≥ 55 years presenting with complaints of cognitive decline and is Conformité Européenne-marked and approved for clinical use by the US FDA. Here, we evaluated the stability of plasma pTau181 measured using the pT181p immunoassay under different pre-analytical and storage conditions in samples from an intended-use population. Methods Whole blood samples from individuals presenting at LMU Hospital with symptom severity ranging from subjective cognitive decline to moderate AD dementia were collected in three different tubes for plasma preparation (Li-Heparin, K2-EDTA, and K3-EDTA). These were transported under cooled (never frozen) conditions to the measurement site and processed within 6 h of collection. Plasma samples were stored at different temperatures for varying durations, and impact on plasma pTau181 recoveries was assessed. Results Out-of-specification results not meeting pre-defined acceptance criteria observed in an initial cohort ( n = 14), were found to be the result of buffy coat/erythrocyte contamination. Pre-analytical procedures were modified to prevent contamination during post-centrifugation plasma transfer. In samples from a separate cohort ( n = 10), no instabilities were observed and acceptance criteria were met. After considering safety margins, analyte stability for all sample types was determined to be 2 days at 25 °C, 7 days at 4 °C, 12 weeks at -20 °C, and 16 weeks at -80°C; stability was also observed after one freeze/thaw cycle. Conclusions pT181p immunoassay measurements were stable and robust with respect to different sample handling procedures and storage conditions. These findings support implementation of the assay into routine, non-specialist healthcare settings to facilitate practical blood-based testing to rule out AD-related Aβ pathology.

title: Plasma p-tau217 in real-world clinical practice: distribution across clinical diagnostic categories, clinician confidence, and impact on care pathways
abstract: Plasma phosphorylated tau at threonine 217 (p-tau217) is a highly accurate blood-based biomarker for Alzheimer’s disease pathology, but evidence regarding its determinants and clinical impact in routine practice remains limited. We evaluated its distribution across real-world clinical phenotypes, biological determinants, and impact on diagnostic pathways. Between January and December 2025, we analyzed 1,368 consecutive patients undergoing plasma p-tau217 testing as part of routine evaluation for cognitive disorders across 24 participating centers in secondary and tertiary care settings. Diagnostic hypotheses were categorized as suspected Alzheimer’s disease, suspected non-Alzheimer cognitive disorders, or cognitive impairment without a specific etiological hypothesis. Plasma p-tau217 was categorized as negative, equivocal, or positive using predefined cut-offs. Associations with age, sex, cognitive status, renal function, and diagnostic group were assessed using descriptive statistics and multivariable models. Available paired CSF biomarker data were retrospectively analyzed. Clinical implementation was evaluated through a prescriber survey and objective activity data. Among 1,368 patients, 997 had suspected Alzheimer’s disease, 180 suspected non-Alzheimer cognitive disorders, and 191 no specific etiological hypothesis. Plasma p-tau217 positivity was higher in suspected Alzheimer’s disease than in suspected non-Alzheimer conditions (66.1% versus 17.8%), whereas patients without a specific hypothesis showed an intermediate distribution. Equivocal results occurred in 19.9% and were more frequent in older individuals. Plasma p-tau217 concentrations increased with age, were higher in women, were inversely correlated with MMSE and renal function, and differed across diagnostic groups. In 117 patients with paired plasma and CSF data, plasma p-tau217 correlated with the CSF p-tau181/Aβ42 ratio (Spearman ρ = 0.640) and showed good discrimination for a positive ratio (> 0.10; AUC = 0.870). Among 53 prescribers, 71% reported increased confidence in plasma p-tau217 since starting to use it, 80% shorter diagnostic delay, and 63% reduced use of brain fluorodeoxyglucose positron emission tomography. Cerebrospinal fluid biomarker requests decreased by approximately 46% between January–June 2024 and July–December 2025. In real-world clinical practice, plasma p-tau217 showed distinct distributions across clinical phenotypes and was associated with measurable changes in diagnostic pathways. Interpretation should integrate patient-specific factors, including age and renal function, together with the clinical context and pre-test probability.

title: Short-interval variability and test-retest reliability of Alzheimer’s disease plasma biomarkers in a clinically heterogenous cohort
abstract: Abstract Background Assessment of short-term within-subject variability and test-retest reliability of Alzheimer’s disease (AD)-related plasma biomarkers is important for real-world clinical implementation and interpretation in research studies. In this study we aimed to assess short-term variability and reliability of core AD plasma biomarkers, proposed ratios, and evaluate a broader proteomic panel. Methods Two serial plasma samples were collected from each of the 92 participants enrolled in observational research studies over intervals ranging from 30 minutes to three months. Test-retest reliability and within-subject variability were assessed for 131 biomarkers measured on three immunoassays (Lumipulse G plasma p-tau217; Fujirebio, NULISAseq CNS Disease Panel and NULISAqpcr AD 5-Plex; Alamar Biosciences). We subsequently evaluated the stability of a dual cut-point approach for AD probability diagnostic categorisation and examined whether within-subject variability was associated with inter-sample interval (time between serial blood sampling). Results All core AD plasma biomarkers assessed in this study (Aβ42, BD-p-tau181, BD-p-tau217, BD-p-tau231, p-tau181, p-tau217, p-tau231, GFAP and NfL) demonstrated strong correlations (r ≥ 0.79) and high reliability (ICC ≥ 0.84). Within-subject variability was moderate to low for core AD plasma biomarkers. Using a validated dual cut-point approach for plasma p-tau217, most individuals (92%) remained within the same diagnostic category (high/indeterminate/low) across both timepoints, and no individual moved across two boundaries (i.e. from high to low AD probability categorisation or vice versa). For the majority of analytes, within-subject variability was not associated with inter-sample interval after adjustment for age and sex, however, the core AD plasma biomarker, NfL did have a significant association. Conclusions While core AD plasma biomarkers had limited variability and high reliability over short-intervals, other central nervous system (CNS)-relevant biomarkers showed greater variability, which may be relevant for interpretation in association studies and clinical applications.

title: Beyond lipidation: CSF APOE4 protein burden, not HDL subclass, drives tau associations in APOE4 Alzheimer’s disease
authors: for the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
abstract: Apolipoprotein E ε4 (APOE4) is the strongest genetic risk factor for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet whether its pathogenic effects are driven by HDL lipidation state or by elevated APOE4 levels in the CNS remains unclear. Using ADNI data, we analyzed cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma small and large HDL particle concentrations, total APOE levels, and isoform-specific APOE3 and APOE4 protein levels in 144 participants with APOE ε3/ε3, ε3/ε4, or ε4/ε4 genotypes, grouped by cognitive state and memory progression over 4 years. Memory loss was defined as ≥ 10% decline on the Rey Auditory Verbal Learning Test (RAVLT) delayed recall between baseline and 48-month follow-up. Cross-sectional associations with CSF Aβ1-42, total tau, and p-tau181 were evaluated using covariate-adjusted linear regression, and longitudinal trajectories were examined using linear mixed-effects models over 6 years. CSF small and large HDL levels were higher in cognitively normal individuals and non-progressors, while APOE4 carriers exhibited reduced CSF small HDL relative to ε3 homozygotes. Importantly, APOE4 status moderated HDL-biomarker associations in opposing directions: in carriers, higher CSF small HDL was associated with lower tau and Aβ1-42, whereas in non-carriers, higher CSF small HDL was associated with higher CSF tau levels. Higher CSF APOE4 protein levels were associated with elevated tau and p-tau181, while plasma APOE measures showed minimal and often opposing associations with CSF biomarkers. Longitudinally, higher baseline CSF APOE4 proportion was associated with greater memory decline over 6 years but did not predict biomarker change. These findings argue against a protective role of APOE4 lipidation in AD and instead support a CNS-compartment model in which APOE4 protein burden aligns more closely with tau pathology and cognitive decline than peripheral APOE or HDL measures.

title: Neuropsychiatric symptoms trajectories preceding incident mild cognitive impairment and dementia
abstract: To characterize nonlinear neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) trajectories preceding mild cognitive impairment (MCI) and dementia and examine their associations with neuropathology and cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) biomarkers. We analyzed 11,781 cognitively normal participants aged 60 years or older from the National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center. NPS were assessed using the Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire and Mild Behavioral Impairment–derived domains. Event-anchored models evaluated the normal-to-MCI and MCI-to-dementia transitions. Among 11,781 participants, 2,865 developed MCI and 731 subsequently developed dementia. Overall NPS separation was already present at the earliest evaluated time point, 12 years before MCI diagnosis (RR = 1.42, 95% CI 1.09–1.84), and first became significant 5 years before dementia diagnosis (RR = 1.41, 95% CI 1.15–1.74). These time points also met the prespecified acceleration criteria, although the 12-year estimate was located at the boundary of the observation window. Emotional dysregulation showed the earliest sustained separation before MCI, whereas domain-specific acceleration preceding dementia was staggered from 5 to 1 years before diagnosis. Autopsy analyses showed heterogeneous associations across Alzheimer Disease–Related Neuropathologic Measures, Lewy Body Pathology, and Cerebrovascular Pathologies. In CSF analyses, only p-tau status was associated with a significant trajectory difference. Distinct nonlinear NPS trajectories preceded MCI and dementia and showed heterogeneous neuropathological correlates. Longitudinal NPS assessment may provide complementary information about behavioral progression, although its individual predictive value requires validation.

title: Gut microbiota depletion modulates cerebrovascular dysfunction in Alzheimer’s disease via IL-17 A/Act1-driven pyroptosis-associated pericyte injury
abstract: Cerebrovascular dysfunction is an early hallmark of Alzheimer’s disease (AD), yet the upstream drivers linking peripheral immunity to neurovascular injury remain elusive. The gut microbiota has emerged as a critical regulator of systemic immunity, but whether and how microbiota-driven immune signals impair the neurovascular unit remains poorly understand. Using APP/PS1 mice and primary mouse cerebral pericytes, we investigated the effects of gut microbiota depletion and IL-17 A neutralization on AD-associated neurovascular dysfunction. We integrated flow cytometry of meningeal immunity, Evans Blue assays for blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity, and molecular analyses of pyroptosis-associated pericyte injury and neurotrophic signaling. Gut microbiota depletion significantly attenuated cerebrovascular rarefaction, restored pericyte coverage, and rescued BBB leakage in APP/PS1 mice. These vascular improvements were accompanied by marked reductions in systemic IL-17 A levels and meningeal CD4 + IL-17 A + T cell accumulation. Mechanistically, IL-17 A induced pyroptosis-associated pericyte injury through an IL-17RA/Act1 dependent signaling cascade involving the NLRP3 inflammasome. Concurrently, IL-17 A signaling suppressed the CREB/BDNF trophic axis, further compromising pericyte survival. Pharmacological neutralization of IL-17 A recapitulated the neurovascular and cognitive protection observed with microbiota depletion, whereas combined interventions yielded no additive effects. Our results identify gut microbiota-associated IL-17 A signaling as a contributor to pyroptosis-associated pericyte injury and neurovascular unit dysfunction in AD, highlighting this pathway as a potential therapeutic target for early intervention.

title: Different profiles of sleep disturbances in early-stage neurocognitive diseases: a prospective cohort study
abstract: Abstract Background Alzheimer’sdisease (AD), behavioral variant frontotemporal dementia bvFTD, and dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) are all associated with sleep disturbances; however, reports on the prevalence of sleep disorders or symptoms in the early stages of these diseases are limited. Our goal was to assess the prevalence of sleep disturbances and characterize different sleep disturbance profiles in early-stage AD, bvFTD and DLB. Methods A total of 111 early-stage patients including 60 AD (mean age 64.3), 35 bvFTD (mean age 62.4), and 16 DLB cases (mean age 71.1), along with 63 cognitively healthy controls (HC, mean age 59.0), were prospectively recruited from Kuopio and Oulu University Hospitals. Early-stage was determined by Clinical Dementia Rating Scale (CDR) global score 0–1. Sleep disturbances were evaluated using the Basic Nordic Sleep Questionnaire (BNSQ), focusing on characterization of prior sleep habits, sleep disorders, and sleep-related (hypnotic) drug usage. Results DLB patients showed the highest overall burden of sleep disturbances relative to other groups. When bvFTD was compared to AD, patients with bvFTD reported more apneas during sleep than AD (18% % vs. 4%, p = 0.024, OR = 0.17, 95% Cl 0.03–0.92). When compared to HC, patients with bvFTD exhibited fewer nighttime awakenings (44% vs. 71%, p = 0.003, OR = 0.22, 95% CI 0.08–0.59) and reported about one hour more sleep per day (8.46 h vs. 7.59 h, General linear model, p = 0.020, B = -0.70), similar to findings in AD (8.40 h vs. General linear model, 7.59 h, p = 0.001, B = -0.78). No significant differences in total sleep duration were observed between disease groups. Conclusions Sleep disturbance profiles differed across disease groups at an early stage, but when compared to HC differences were modest. These findings suggest sleep disturbances may be present in early disease stage.

title: Differences in Alzheimer’s disease biomarkers between African American and White participants across cerebrospinal fluid and plasma: a systematic review and meta-analysis
abstract: Abstract Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) biomarkers are essential for early diagnosis in clinical practice and research. However, current diagnostic frameworks were developed primarily in White cohorts, raising concerns about generalizability. We evaluated differences in AD biomarkers between African American and White participants in cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) and plasma. Methods In this systematic review and meta-analysis, we searched PubMed, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science, and the Cochrane Library (inception to June 25, 2025). We included studies comparing amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration biomarkers between African American and White participants. Random-effects meta-analyses were performed using standardized mean differences (SMDs). Subgroup analyses were conducted by biomarker type, matrix, and cognitive status. This study is registered with PROSPERO, CRD420251242112. Results Eighteen studies comprising 13,191 participants (3,171 African American and 10,020 White) were included in this analysis. Compared with White participants, African American participants had significantly lower levels of CSF total tau (average SMD − 0.51, 95% CI -0.65 to -0.36), phosphorylated tau181 (SMD − 0.42, 95% CI -0.54 to -0.31), and neurofilament light chain (SMD − 0.21, 95% CI -0.30 to -0.12). In plasma, phosphorylated tau181 (SMD − 0.20, 95% CI -0.33 to -0.07) and neurofilament light chain (SMD − 0.63, 95% CI -1.14 to -0.11) levels were also significantly lower in African American participants. Plasma Aβ42 and Aβ40 were also lower and the plasma Aβ42/40 ratio higher (SMD 0.37, 95% CI 0.06 to 0.68). In CSF, the Aβ42/40 ratio was higher at the threshold of significance (SMD 0.23, 95% CI 0.00 to 0.46; three comparisons), whereas CSF Aβ42 did not differ. Conclusion African American participants exhibit consistently lower tau-related and neurodegeneration biomarker levels in both CSF and plasma, with amyloid differences in the same direction in both compartments but stronger in plasma. Whether these differences reflect true variation in underlying pathology or compartment-specific biomarker behavior cannot be determined without paired gold-standard measures such as amyloid positron emission tomography or neuropathology. These findings are hypothesis-generating and support cautious, multimodal interpretation rather than uniform application of diagnostic thresholds derived predominantly from White cohorts. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420251242112.

title: Effect of high-risk SORL1 variants on clinical presentation in symptomatic Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Background Rare, high-risk variants in SORL1 are established genetic contributors to Alzheimer’s disease (AD), but their impact on clinical presentation remains uncharacterized. This study investigates the effect of rare high-risk SORL1 variant ( SORL1 hi ) carriers on the clinical presentation, cognitive decline and time from diagnosis to death in symptomatic AD. Methods Patients with a biomarker-confirmed diagnosis of symptomatic AD and available genetic information ( n = 1546, age at diagnosis 64.3 ± 7, 52% female, 69% APOE ε4 carriers) were included from the Amsterdam Dementia Cohort. SORL1 hi carriers were identified per established criteria, and wild-type (WT) carriers ( n = 1511) served as controls. Baseline assessments included family history, neuropsychological testing, cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) AD core biomarkers (Aβ42, pTau-181, total tau), MRI visual rating (Fazekas) and quantitative analysis of cortical thickness and subcortical volumes and EEG ratings. Longitudinal data on cognitive decline (median interval 2.1 years, interquartile range (IQR) 1.1–3.4) and time between diagnosis and death (median 7.0 years, IQR 6.7–7.2) were collected. Associations of SORL1 hi carriers with these variables were analyzed using linear, logistic, Cox regression models, as well as linear mixed-effects models, adjusting for age, sex and education, with exploratory analyses stratified by APOE ε4 status. Results We identified 35 SORL1 hi carriers, with 28 unique variants (21 missense, 6 protein truncating, 1 in-frame insertion). Compared with WT, SORL1 hi carriers more often had an affected first-degree relative (71% vs. 45%, P = 0.006). Carriers were comparable to WT in terms of MMSE at baseline and MMSE decline over time, neuropsychological profiles, CSF biomarkers, MRI measures, EEG, and mortality rate after diagnosis. Stratified analyses showed that SORL1 hi ε4 non-carriers showed higher CSF pTau-181 and t-Tau biomarker concentrations and had a shorter time to death than WT ε4 non-carriers. Discussion SORL1 hi variant carriers presented with a clinical endophenotype comparable to symptomatic WT AD patients, suggesting that SORL1 genetic deficits can result in a typical AD end-stage. These findings support targeting SORL1-mediated pathways as an out-of-the-box, but viable strategy for AD. Future studies should characterize the biological changes in presymptomatic SORL1 hi carriers in comparison to sporadic AD. These findings highlight that genetic screening is essential to identify SORL1 carriers in clinical practice.

title: Brain-derived extracellular vesicle profiling in Down syndrome-associated Alzheimer’s disease
abstract: Abstract Background Brain-derived extracellular vesicles (BDEVs) offer a non-invasive window into central nervous system pathology, but their molecular characterization across the Down syndrome (DS)—associated Alzheimer’s disease continuum (DSAD) remains unexplored. Methods We enriched plasma neuron- and astrocyte-derived EVs (NDEVs and ADEVs) from 57 individuals: 14 controls and 43 individuals with DS (20 asymptomatic and 23 symptomatic for AD). The ultrasensitive 127-plex CNS-NULISAseq panel was applied to profile these BDEVs subpopulations. We benchmarked NULISAseq analytical sensitivity against the Olink platform in ADEVs, characterized BDEV differential proteomic profiles across clinical groups, and correlated the findings with established plasma AD biomarkers (pTau217, NfL, and GFAP). Results NULISAseq demonstrated superior analyte detectability in ADEVs (87.4%) compared to the 11.9% observed in a previous Olink-based study using the same ADEV isolation protocol in an independent cohort. BDEV characterization revealed signatures of neurodegeneration, inflammation, and vascular/metabolic stress. Notably, FLT1 in ADEVs, and CXCL10, NEFH, PGK1, and NPY in NDEVs, were elevated in DS and significantly correlated with established plasma AD biomarkers. Moreover, group comparisons revealed stage-associated increases in these NDEV markers across the DSAD continuum. Conclusions This study supports multiplex profiling of BDEVs as a non-invasive window into central nervous system biology, providing biological information that complements current plasma biomarkers and offering novel insights into the molecular mechanisms driving DSAD.

title: Cognitive impairment, medial temporal lobe changes, and fluid biomarkers of Alzheimer’s disease and neurodegeneration following herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis
abstract: Abstract Background Herpesvirus encephalitis is a severe brain infection, in adults most often caused by herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1). It predominantly affects the medial temporal lobes (MTL), which are critical for memory functions. Links have been discussed between herpes virus infections and Alzheimer’s disease (AD). We therefore investigated cognitive function, structural brain changes, and fluid biomarkers related to AD and other neurodegenerative processes in individuals with previous herpes simplex virus type 1 encephalitis (HSE). Methods Eleven patients with prior HSE were retrospectively identified using a clinical CSF laboratory database. Control groups included 44 cognitively unimpaired (CU) individuals, 44 mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and 22 AD dementia patients from the Swedish BioFINDER-2 study. Groups were stratified by amyloid-β (Aβ) status using CSF Aβ42/Aβ40. All participants underwent neuropsychological testing. Structural brain changes were assessed using 7T or 3T MRI including visual evaluation of lesions and automated segmentation of MTL subregions. Plasma biomarkers (tau phosphorylated at position 217 (p-tau217), p-tau181, glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP), and neurofilament light (NfL)) were measured using immunoassays. Results The mean follow-up time since infection was 6.5 years. The encephalitis group (mean age 49 years, 55% females) was age-matched to the CU Aβ- group but younger than other groups. MRI findings in the encephalitis group ranged from marked unilateral MTL atrophy to no visible changes. Compared with CU individuals, encephalitis patients showed significantly impaired episodic memory (delayed recall) and lower global cognition, comparable to MCI but less severe than AD dementia. Within the encephalitis group, episodic memory impairment was associated with visually assessed MTL atrophy ( p = 0.0185). In hemispheres without gross atrophy, MTL subregional volumes resembled CU and MCI but were larger than in AD dementia. Plasma p-tau217 and GFAP levels were elevated in the full HSE-group compared with Aβ-negative CU and MCI, but lower than in AD dementia. P-tau181 and NfL levels were similar to CU. P-tau217 was not significantly different between Aβ-negative HSE and Aβ-negative CU. Associations between GFAP and cognitive performance were no longer significant after exclusion of the two patients with Fazekas grade 3 white matter lesions. Conclusions Previous HSE was associated with substantial heterogeneity in long-term cognitive performance, with poorer delayed recall associated with longer time since infection. Cognitive findings were also related to focal MTL atrophy, supporting a contribution of structural injury to long-term cognitive outcomes. Only a minority of the patients had signs of AD pathology by CSF biomarkers. Larger longitudinal studies are needed to determine the trajectories and mechanisms of cognitive change following HSE.
